summary: Multipoint LDP identifies a root node by address, and intermediate routers must find a route to it. That fails when the route is a BGP route and the core is BGP-free. This RFC defines procedures to build multipoint LSPs in that situation.

plainLanguage.summary: Directions for a delivery tree point to a faraway town, but middle roads do not have a map to it. This gives them a way to find the way anyway.

questions: how to build p2mp lsp without a route to the root
what is a recursive opaque value in mldp
how does mldp work in a bgp-free core
what is the vpn-recursive opaque value
subtitle: How multipoint LDP can build trees through a core that has no route to the tree's root, by wrapping the real root inside the opaque value.

tldr.problem: Multipoint LDP identifies a tree by its root node address, and every router must look that address up in its routing table. In a BGP-free core, interior routers have no route to a root learned through BGP.
tldr.mechanism: The edge router swaps the root for an address the core does know, such as the BGP next hop, and tucks the original FEC element inside a new Recursive Opaque Value. The router at the new root unwraps it and continues with the original.
tldr.outcome: Multipoint LSPs can be built across a BGP-free core, across non-segmented inter-AS option B VPN setups, and in a limited carrier's carrier service.

today: RFC 6512 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on mLDP in RFC 6388 and the multicast VPN procedures in RFC 6513.

sections.title: The Problem: No Route to the Root
sections.content:
Multipoint LDP (mLDP) from RFC 6388 extends LDP (RFC 5036) to build Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) and Multipoint-to-Multipoint (MP2MP) Label Switched Paths, together called MP LSPs. An MP LSP is identified by a root node plus a variable-length opaque value. The root has a special job: mLDP messages about an LSP are forwarded to the LDP adjacency that is the next hop on the route to the root.

That breaks when the LSP must cross a part of the network with no route to the root. In the RFC's example topology, PE1 has a BGP-learned route for a customer router R, with BGP next hop PE2, but interior routers such as P1 and P2 hold no BGP routes and cannot reach R. If CE1 hands PE1 a FEC element with R as root, PE1 cannot pass it unchanged to P1.

What is needed is a way for PE1 to ask P1 to build the LSP as if PE2 were the root, for PE2 to know the LSP is really rooted at R, and for PE2 to recover the original FEC element and pass it on to CE2.
sections.plainLanguage: The roads in the middle of the country do not have a map to the far-away house. We need a trick so they can still help deliver the parcel.

sections.title: The Recursive Opaque Value
sections.content: The fix is a new kind of opaque value, the Recursive Opaque Value, a basic type identified by a 1-octet type field with Type = 7. Its value field is itself a complete P2MP or MP2MP FEC element, encoded exactly as RFC 6388 specifies, with its own type, length and value. So the length of the Recursive Opaque Value includes the type, length and value fields of the contained element.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a box that has another, complete label and parcel inside it.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
Suppose CE1 sends PE1 a FEC element with root R and opaque value Q, called CE1-FEC. PE1 finds that R matches a BGP route with next hop PE2, and knows from its configuration that the routers on the path to PE2 are BGP-free. PE1 builds PE2-FEC, with root PE2 and the opaque value being a Recursive Opaque Value containing CE1-FEC, and sends it to P1.

Interior routers see only a request to build an MP LSP rooted at PE2. They MUST NOT interpret the opaque value at all. When PE2-FEC reaches PE2, PE2 sees that it is the root and that the opaque value is a Recursive Opaque Value, so it MUST replace PE2-FEC with the contents, CE1-FEC, before any further processing. CE1-FEC then goes on to CE2 and R. The presumption is that PE2 has a route to the root named in CE1-FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The middle offices just move the big box toward the town they know. In that town the box is opened and the original parcel goes on its way.

sections.title: The VPN-Recursive Opaque Value
sections.content: When MP LSPs carry the multicast traffic of a VPN (RFC 6513), a second type is needed: the VPN-Recursive Opaque Value, with Type = 8. Its value field is an 8-octet Route Distinguisher (RD) followed by a P2MP or MP2MP FEC element encoded as in RFC 6388. Its length therefore covers the 8 octets of RD plus the type, length and value fields of the contained element.
sections.plainLanguage: This box has the same parcel inside, plus a small tag saying which customer's mail it belongs to.

sections.title: Where the VPN Variant Is Used
sections.content:
Non-segmented inter-AS P-tunnels. In an inter-AS option B VPN interconnect, the first AS's border router (ASBR1) has no route to PE routers in other ASes, and the multicast VPN policy uses mLDP with non-segmented inter-AS P-tunnels. To join an LSP rooted at PE2, PE1 knows only that ASBR1 is the BGP next hop. It builds <root=ASBR1, opaque_value=<root=PE2, RD, opaque_value=Q>>, taking the RD from the NLRI of the Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route originated by PE2. When ASBR1 receives it, it extracts PE2. If it has a route to PE2, it continues with <root=PE2, opaque_value=Q>. If not, it looks up the Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route for PE2 and that RD, finds the next hop (say ASBR2) and continues with a FEC element rooted at ASBR2 and carrying the unchanged VPN-Recursive element. This gives mLDP P-tunnels the functionality that the MVPN Join Attribute gives PIM P-tunnels.

Limited carrier's carrier. When PE1 and PE2 offer Carrier's Carrier VPN Service, PE1 looks up R in a VRF and finds a VPN-IP route with an RD and next hop PE2. The new FEC element has PE2 as root and a VPN-Recursive Opaque Value holding that RD followed by CE1-FEC. PE2, receiving it over a VRF interface, MUST replace it with CE1-FEC and use the VRF to look up the path to R. The RD also keeps the FEC element unique inside the inner carrier's network.

This only works when both carriers use non-segmented mLDP P-tunnels and the inner carrier does not aggregate the outer carrier's P-tunnels, instead carrying each in a single P-tunnel of its own. The two scenarios are told apart by the fact that carrier's carrier mLDP messages travel on VRF interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The same boxed-parcel trick works between different countries' post offices and for a big mail company that carries a smaller one's mail, as long as everyone follows the rules.

sections.title: IANA Code Points
sections.content: RFC 6388 defines a registry for the LDP MP Opaque Value Element Basic Type. Two new code points were assigned there: Recursive Opaque Value as Type 7, a TLV that encodes an mLDP FEC type, and VPN-Recursive Opaque Value as Type 8, an 8-octet Route Distinguisher (as in RFC 4364) followed by a TLV that encodes an mLDP FEC type.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new box types were given official numbers, 7 and 8, in a public list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of LDP and mLDP apply. Unauthorized modification of the FEC elements defined here can disrupt multipoint LSP creation or make LSPs pass through parts of the network where they should not go, which could be part of an attack to insert or intercept multicast traffic. The RFC argues that these elements are not inherently more vulnerable than earlier FEC elements, so it adds no new vulnerabilities. General MPLS security issues are described in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone tampering with the box labels could send mail the wrong way. That risk was already there before, and the new boxes are no easier to tamper with.
